Remodeling · Chicago and the south suburbs

When the job turns out to be more than paint.

Plenty of jobs turn out to be something else once somebody looks underneath. The bathroom needs painting, and the floor by the tub has a soft spot. The trim needs repainting, and the sill behind it has gone. Most painters stop there and hand you a list of people to call. We do the carpentry, the tile, the flooring, the subfloors and the concrete as well, across Chicago and the south and southwest suburbs, so the job keeps moving instead of sitting half finished while you chase somebody else.

Sound familiar

Most people call us for one of these reasons

If one of these is roughly your situation, you are in the right place.

  • A painter has already told you it is not a painting job. That usually means rot, a soft floor, or a wall that has to be rebuilt before anything can be coated. All of that is work we do, and it is the reason this page exists.
  • You have been trying to get three trades to line up. Subfloor, then tile, then trim, then paint. Three companies and three calendars is why that project has taken four months. One company is one calendar.
  • It started as one room and grew. Bathrooms and kitchens do this constantly. The honest move is to look at all of it at once and tell you the real size of the job at the quote, not on day two.
  • You want to know whether it is even worth doing. Sometimes the answer is that the job belongs with a specialist, or that it is not worth the money this year. If that is the true answer, you will hear it.

How the job runs

What happens, in the order it happens

  1. Look at the whole thingA bathroom that needs painting sometimes needs the floor pulled up first. Finding that out at the quote is better than finding it out on day two.
  2. Say what it actually isIf a job is bigger than you were hoping, you get told at the quote. If it is smaller, you get told that too.
  3. One company, one scheduleThe reason this list exists is sequencing. Subfloor, then tile, then trim, then paint, in that order, run off one calendar instead of three companies coordinating diaries.
  4. Finish itIncluding the painting, which is the part that usually gets left when a remodeler hands over.

The part you cannot see

What good preparation is, and why the cheap quote is cheap

On a remodel the surprises are never in the finish work. They are underneath it. So the part worth paying for is the looking, and that has to happen before the quote rather than after the demolition.

  1. Protecting the rest of the houseDust from tile and drywall work travels through a whole house through the return vents. Doorways get sealed, the route in and out gets covered, and the vents in the work area get taped off before anything gets broken up.
  2. Taking it apart carefullyDemolition looks like the fun part and it is where most of the accidental damage happens. Tile comes off without wrecking the wall behind it, and trim that is going back on comes off in one piece.
  3. Making the substrate right before the finish goes onTile laid over a soft or uneven subfloor cracks its grout inside a year, however good the tile is. The floor gets made flat and solid first, and that is the part that never shows up in a photograph of a finished bathroom.
  4. Dealing with the water firstIn a bathroom or a basement, whatever is letting water in gets sorted out before anything is closed up over it. Otherwise you are paying to bury the problem somewhere you can no longer reach it.
  5. Prepping the new work for paintNew trim and new drywall need filling, caulking and priming before they take a finish coat, exactly like any other paint job. Skipping that is why new work sometimes looks worse than the old work next to it.

Where a cheap quote saves its money

On bigger jobs the low quote is usually the one that did not look underneath. It is a real price for a smaller job than the one you have, and the difference comes back as a change order once the floor is up and you have nowhere else to go. A quote that tells you in advance what happens if there is rot is worth more than a cheaper one that says nothing about it.

What moves the number

Why two quotes for the same job can look nothing alike

There are no prices on this site, because a real number needs somebody standing in front of the work. What we can tell you is what actually drives it, so you can read any quote you get and understand what you are looking at.

  1. What is underneathAlmost every remodeling surprise is under something. Soft subfloor, rot behind trim, and old work done badly are the three usual ones.
  2. How many trades the job needsSequencing several trades on one schedule is the value here, and it is also what makes the number bigger than a paint quote.
  3. Materials you chooseTile, flooring and hardware ranges are wide. That part is genuinely your decision and it moves the total a long way.
  4. Whether anything structural is involvedSome things are not a remodeling job and need the right professional. You will be told which is which.

Ask everybody who quotes you these three questions

What preparation is included. How many coats. What happens to the price if the preparation turns out worse than it looks. The answers tell you far more than the total at the bottom does.

Questions

What people ask about remodeling and trades

Are you a painter or a remodeler?

Mostly a painter, which is why painting is what this site leads with. The rest of the trade list is real work that gets done here, and it exists so a job does not stop when it turns out to need more than paint.

Why does that matter to me?

Because the common version of this goes: a painter finds a rotten sill, stops, and you spend two weeks finding a carpenter who will take a small job. One contractor who can do both is not a bigger company, it is a shorter calendar.

Do you do full kitchen and bathroom remodels?

Ask. Some are a good fit and some are better off with a company that does nothing else. You will get a straight answer about which one yours is rather than a yes to everything.

Do you do tile and subfloors?

Yes. Worth saying plainly because almost nobody else in this market offers tile or subfloor work alongside painting, and a soft floor under a tiled bathroom is one of the most common jobs that gets bounced between contractors.

Who actually does the work?

We do, and the owner runs it. Mike Walsh quotes the job himself and stays on it while our crew works, rather than handing it to a branch office and a salesperson. That is not something a franchise can copy, and it is the main reason people call back.
